elements.text: Leakage runs through the whole stack
Leakage has four layers, not just training
P = f( LLM, prompt, scaffold, tools, retriever, memory, environment )

"The model was not trained on the test set" is nowhere near sufficient: any one component of the stack can carry benchmark information. Realistic tools enlarge the leakage surface, and a benchmark may be searchable.
The nine entry points are where a benchmark can leak in: the model, the fine-tuning, the prompt, the retriever, the memory, the web, the environment, the scaffold and the developer.

slides.title: Two challenges with how agents are evaluated

elements.text: SINGLE TURN, AND SUCCESS RATE ALONE
Two challenges with how agents are evaluated

Most benchmarks give one fully-specified instruction, with no user in the loop, while real work is ambiguous, revised and interrupted.
Single-turn scoring rewards confident guessing: asking a clarifying question costs steps and earns no credit.
The three questions to ask instead
The same success rate, one bad outcome and one good one.

Non-determinism makes a single-run score noise rather than signal.
Outcome-only scoring passes lucky or unsafe runs; trajectory matching fails valid ones.
Ask two questions of any benchmark: is there a user in the loop, and what else is measured besides success?
HOW FAST THE FRONTIER CATCHES THE HUMAN BASELINE
Saturated means the frontier reached the human baseline, or the top models stopped separating.

Evaluation is still evolving toward stateful, long-horizon, multi-grader, contamination-aware measurement.
The 2025-2026 era already shows the move: larger scope, less specific instructions, more realistic use cases.
The newest era is the least saturated: GDPval, BrowseComp, Terminal-Bench and ARC-AGI-3 are the four benchmarks of 2025-2026.
A benchmark is a protocol, not just a dataset: version and split, permitted tools, budget and grader have to travel with every number.
Six dimensions: objective evaluated, interaction, grader, dataset, main metric, primary concern.

slides.title: A real agent has more than one dimension

elements.text: A real agent has more than one dimension
A dominates B if A is no worse on any metric and better on at least one.
Assignment 3 is evaluated on all three metrics - capability, cost and speed - using exactly this rule.
Better agents are not simply cheaper or faster: they are Pareto-efficient on capability, cost and speed at the same time.
This is the hinge from measurement to the next lecture: once success rate is not enough, cost and latency have to be scored too.
Evaluate the whole stack, not the model: leakage enters through prompt, retrieval, memory, tools, scaffold and developer iteration.
Always ask what a benchmark grades; single-turn final-answer scoring misses exactly the behaviour real work needs.
Benchmarks saturate in months, so treat them as a moving target and measure capability, cost and speed together.
The benchmark tour is organised by what the grader inspects: final answer, calls, DB state, patch tests, final system state, checkpoints.
Ask that question before you ask what the score is.
